title: AI vs AI: When Attackers Use LLMs for Phishing

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Rachel, there's a narrative going around about ai security that I think misses the mark. People either think it's overhyped or they think it's going to change everything overnight. Where does the truth actually lie?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: (laughs) That's the perfect framing, because the truth is always in between. What's happening with when attackers use llms for phishing is real — it's not hype. But it's also not overnight. We've been working on this for years, and what people are seeing now is the result of a lot of unglamorous engineering and science that happened behind the scenes.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Welcome to TechNova. I'm Dr. Sarah Chen.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: And I'm Marcus Webb. Today we're joined by Rachel Tobac, CEO & Ethical Hacker at SocialProof Security. Rachel, welcome to the show.

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: Thanks for having me. Really glad to be here.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Rachel, give us the honest state of ai security in Cybersecurity as of mid-2026. Not the hype version — the real version.

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: The honest version is that we're at an inflection point. The breakthroughs in threat landscape evolution and zero-day economics over the past eighteen months have been genuine — not just press releases, but real technical progress that you can measure. The key thing that's changed is AI-powered attacks has gone from theoretical to practical. We're no longer asking 'can this work?' — we're asking 'how do we scale it?'

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: What does that scaling look like in concrete terms?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: It means we're moving from bench-scale demonstrations to real-world deployment. The numbers I can share: we're seeing improvements in defensive AI that are orders of magnitude better than where we were two years ago. And critically, the cost curve is bending in the right direction. When you combine better performance with lower cost, you get adoption, and that's what's happening now.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What surprised you most in the last year?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: The speed. I expected progress, but the pace has been remarkable. supply chain risks advanced faster than I predicted, and regulatory compliance turned out to be more tractable than we thought. When you have multiple breakthroughs happening simultaneously, they compound on each other, and that's when you get these nonlinear jumps.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Rachel, let's talk about what's still hard. What are the problems that keep you up at night?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: The biggest one is workforce shortage. It's the difference between something that works in the lab and something that works in production, every day, under real conditions. We've solved the science. What we haven't fully solved is the engineering — cloud security, incident response, and the integration of all these components into a reliable system. That's the 80 percent of the work that nobody sees.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Can you give us a specific example of a problem you had to solve?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: Sure. Take encryption and PQC — six months ago, we were hitting a wall there. The conventional approach wasn't working, and we had to rethink the problem from scratch. What we ended up doing was phishing-centric — we restructured the entire approach around that, and it unlocked everything else. Sometimes the breakthrough isn't a new technique — it's a new framing of the problem.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: How many people are working on these problems at your level?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: Globally? Maybe a few hundred people who truly understand the cutting edge. It's a small field, and the expertise is concentrated in a handful of teams. That's both a challenge and an opportunity — it means progress is bottlenecked by talent, but it also means that a single breakthrough from one team can advance the entire field.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Rachel, who else is working in this space, and how does your approach differ?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: There are several serious players. Some are taking the threat landscape evolution route, which is well-established but has limitations. Others are betting on zero-day economics, which is newer and riskier but potentially more powerful. Our approach is different because we prioritize AI-powered attacks — most teams optimize for peak performance, but we optimize for reliability and cost at scale. That's what matters for real-world deployment.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Is this a winner-take-all market?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: I don't think so. The market is large and diverse enough that different approaches will win in different segments. The real competition isn't between the companies in this space — it's between ai security and the incumbent technology. We're all fighting to prove this is better than what exists today, and there's room for multiple winners once we do that.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What about the investment environment? Is there enough capital flowing in?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: The capital is there — maybe too much, in some ways. The risk isn't lack of funding. It's that funding without focus leads to wasted effort. The companies that will succeed are the ones that can turn capital into concrete milestones — not more press releases, but real technical progress that moves the needle.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Rachel, what should people be watching for in the next twelve to eighteen months?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: Three things. First, defensive AI — we'll see meaningful progress there, and it'll be measurable. Second, supply chain risks — there are developments coming that the public doesn't know about yet, and they'll change the conversation. Third, the policy and regulatory side — regulatory compliance is going to become a much bigger topic as the technology matures.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: If you could give one piece of advice to someone listening who's trying to understand where Cybersecurity is heading, what would it be?

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: Don't trust the extremes — neither the hype that says everything changes tomorrow, nor the skepticism that says nothing will ever work. The truth is in the middle, and it's moving faster than most people realize. The best thing you can do is engage with the actual data — read the papers, look at the numbers, talk to the practitioners. The signal is there if you know where to look.

lines.speaker: Marcus Webb
lines.text: Rachel Tobac, CEO & Ethical Hacker at SocialProof Security. Thank you so much for joining us today.

lines.speaker: Rachel Tobac
lines.text: Thank you both. This was a really enjoyable conversation.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: And thanks to all of you for listening. This is TechNova — see you next time.
